title: HE HAD NO SONS… SO HE GAVE HIS DAUGHTER TO HIS EGYPTIAN SERVANT. BUT THE FAMILY LINE THAT FOLLOWED REVEALS SOMETHING WE CANNOT AFFORD TO MISS.
paragraphs: HE HAD NO SONS… SO HE GAVE HIS DAUGHTER TO HIS EGYPTIAN SERVANT. BUT THE FAMILY LINE THAT FOLLOWED REVEALS SOMETHING WE CANNOT AFFORD TO MISS.

Buried inside a genealogy most Christians skip is a father facing the end of his family line, an Egyptian servant whose name Scripture refused to erase, and a daughter whose marriage became part of a remarkable legacy. What happened in 1 Chronicles 2:34–35 challenges our assumptions about status, belonging, and the God who can write a future where everyone else sees a dead end.
There are Bible verses that make you shout.
There are Bible verses that make you weep.
And then there are Bible verses you almost never notice because they are buried between names you cannot pronounce, inside genealogies you are tempted to skip.
But what if one of those forgotten verses contains a story that could change the way you see your own life?
What if a man whose family line appeared to be approaching a dead end became the doorway to an unexpected future?
What if an Egyptian servant, someone whose social position seemed to place him on the margins of the household, became the father of a continuing family line?

And what if God allowed their names to be preserved in Scripture so that thousands of years later, someone who feels overlooked, disqualified, or forgotten might stop and remember that human status is not the final measure of a person's worth?
Because hidden in 1 Chronicles is a sentence that deserves more than a passing glance.

“Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha. Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha his servant, and she bore him Attai.” — 1 Chronicles 2:34–35, translated from the Hebrew
Read it again.
Slowly.
Sheshan had no sons.
He had daughters.
He had an Egyptian servant named Jarha.
And he gave his daughter in marriage to that servant.
Then a child was born.
Attai.
One sentence about a family limitation.
One sentence about an unexpected marriage.
One sentence about a new generation.
And then the genealogy continues.
But before we rush into a dramatic interpretation, we need to understand something important.

The Bible does not tell us that Sheshan's daughter was unwanted. It does not say Jarha was despised. It does not describe a romantic courtship, a secret conversation, or the daughter's private feelings about the marriage.
We must not invent those things and call them Scripture.
The actual account is brief, but what it reveals is remarkable enough without embellishment.
In a society where family descent, inheritance, and household continuity were significant concerns, Sheshan had no male child to continue his immediate line through a son.
And yet his family story did not end there.
That is where the passage begins to speak to something deeply human.
Because sometimes the most painful sentence in your life is not what you lost.
It is what you never received.
The child you prayed for.
The marriage that never happened.
The opportunity that passed you by.
The reconciliation you waited years to see.
The door that stayed closed even after you fasted, prayed, cried, and begged God to open it.
You watched other people celebrate the very thing you were still waiting for.
You congratulated them.
You smiled in photographs.
You whispered, “Praise God.”
And then you went home carrying a question you were almost ashamed to ask.
“Lord, what about me?”
Maybe your story is not about having no sons.
Maybe it is about having no answers.
No direction.
No peace.
No strength left to pretend that everything is fine.
And that is why those first words deserve our attention.
Sheshan had no sons.
In Hebrew, the passage begins:
וְלֹא־הָיָה לְשֵׁשָׁן בָּנִים כִּי אִם־בָּנוֹת
Ve-lo hayah le-Sheshan banim ki im banot.
The meaning is straightforward:
“Now Sheshan had no sons, but daughters.”
The Hebrew word בָּנִים (banim) means “sons,” while בָּנוֹת (banot) means “daughters.”
Notice what the text actually says.
It does not say Sheshan had no children.
It says he had no sons.
That distinction matters.
His daughters were not nothing.
They were not invisible to God.
The genealogy records their existence even though it does not give us the name of the particular daughter who married Jarha.
The absence of a son was a genealogical circumstance, not proof that Sheshan's daughters were failures or that God regarded them as inferior.
And we need to be especially careful here because the Bible must never be used to suggest that a daughter is a disappointment simply because she is not a son.
Genesis 1:27 teaches that both male and female bear God's image.
Their dignity is not dependent on family expectations.
Their worth does not rise or fall with cultural preferences.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to hear that more than anything else today.
You are not worth less because you were not what someone expected.
Maybe you were the daughter who was constantly compared to a son.
Maybe you were the child whose achievements never seemed sufficient.
Maybe you grew up feeling that you had to earn affection by becoming someone else.
Maybe people loved the version of you they imagined more than the person you actually were.
But your dignity was never theirs to create.
God made human beings in His image.
And no human disappointment can erase what the Creator has declared about human worth.
Now look at the next part of the account.
“And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, whose name was Jarha.”
The Hebrew reads:
וּלְשֵׁשָׁן עֶבֶד מִצְרִי וּשְׁמוֹ יַרְחָע
U-le-Sheshan eved Mitsri u-shemo Yarcha.
The phrase identifies Jarha as an Egyptian servant.
The Hebrew word עֶבֶד (eved) can describe a servant or slave, depending on the context.
That means we should not soften the historical reality by pretending Jarha was simply a modern employee who could freely resign whenever he wished.
Ancient servitude involved unequal power, and the text does not explain Jarha's precise legal circumstances or how he came into Sheshan's household.
We should not romanticize those inequalities.
But neither should we overlook the unusual detail the chronicler preserved.
His name was Jarha.
Not merely “the Egyptian.”
Not merely “the servant.”
Jarha.
A man with a name.
A man with a place in this family's recorded history.
And that detail becomes especially striking when we remember the complicated relationship between Israel and Egypt.
Egypt was the land where Israel's ancestors had suffered oppression before the Lord delivered them in the Exodus.
Yet Scripture also contains laws commanding Israel not to despise Egyptians simply because they were Egyptians.
Deuteronomy 23:7 says:
“You shall not abhor an Egyptian, because you were a sojourner in his land.” — ESV
That command does not erase Egypt's oppression of Israel.
It demonstrates that Israel's memory of suffering was not intended to become permission for indiscriminate hatred of every Egyptian.
And in 1 Chronicles, here is an Egyptian man whose name is preserved within a Judahite family genealogy.
His nationality is mentioned.
His servant status is mentioned.
His marriage is mentioned.
His son is mentioned.
And the descendants continue.
We are not told that Jarha's social status automatically changed when he married Sheshan's daughter. We are not given enough information to reconstruct the legal arrangements.
But we are told that he became part of the family line being recorded.
The genealogy does not conceal his Egyptian identity.
It includes it.
Think about that.
How many people spend their entire lives trying to hide the circumstances they came from?
The family background they cannot change.
The poverty they endured.
The shame other people attached to their name.
The place where they were born.
The mistakes of their parents.
The years when nobody took them seriously.
Some people walk into a room already convinced that everyone else belongs there more than they do.
They laugh a little too loudly to hide their insecurity.
They apologize when they have done nothing wrong.
They hesitate to speak because they have spent years being made to feel small.
And eventually, they begin to confuse the way people treated them with the way God sees them.
But listen carefully.
Your social position is not the measure of your soul.
Your salary is not your identity.
Your surname is not your righteousness.
Your nationality does not determine whether you are worthy of human dignity.
And the approval of influential people is not the same thing as the approval of God.
Jarha's story does not prove that every overlooked person will receive a dramatic promotion or marry into a wealthy household.
That would be a promise the passage never makes.
What it does show is that someone identified as an Egyptian servant was not omitted from this recorded family history.
And that should make us cautious about deciding whose life is too insignificant to matter.
Because the God of Scripture repeatedly calls His people to notice those whom society is tempted to overlook.
The poor.
The foreigner.
The widow.
The orphan.
The powerless.
The person who cannot repay our kindness.
James 2:1 warns believers against showing favoritism while claiming faith in Jesus Christ.
And James 2:9 goes further, identifying partiality as sin.
That means we cannot claim to honor the Lord Jesus while treating people as though their value depends on money, influence, ethnicity, or social rank.
Now comes the turning point.
“Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha his servant.”
The Hebrew states:
וַיִּתֵּן שֵׁשָׁן אֶת־בִּתּוֹ לְיַרְחָע עַבְדּוֹ לְאִשָּׁה
Vayitten Sheshan et-bitto le-Yarcha avdo le-ishah.
The expression לְאִשָּׁה (le-ishah) means “as a wife” or “in marriage.”
This is a marriage statement.
It is not simply an account of a servant being rewarded with property.

Nevertheless, because the text does not record the daughter's perspective, we must resist the temptation to describe the marriage as a beautiful romance or assume details about her consent that Scripture does not supply.
Her voice is not recorded.
And that silence should make us humble.
But the genealogy makes the outcome clear.
Sheshan's daughter married Jarha.
And they had a son named Attai.
What appeared to be a genealogical dead end was followed by another generation.
Then another.
And another.
Read 1 Chronicles 2:36–41.
Attai fathered Nathan.
Nathan fathered Zabad.
Zabad fathered Ephlal.
Ephlal fathered Obed.
Obed fathered Jehu.
Jehu fathered Azariah.
And the line continued through Helez, Eleasah, Sismai, Shallum, Jekamiah, and Elishama.
Names.
Generation after generation.
A family line that did not end with the statement, “Sheshan had no sons.”
Now imagine if we had stopped reading at verse 34.
We would have seen the limitation but missed the continuation.
We would have noticed what was absent but not what followed.
We would have read about what Sheshan did not have and never discovered what the genealogy went on to record.
And isn't that exactly what despair does to us?
It makes one painful chapter feel like the entire book.
One rejection becomes “Nobody will ever love me.”
One failure becomes “I will never succeed.”
One betrayal becomes “I can never trust again.”
One season of unanswered prayer becomes “God has abandoned me.”
One sin becomes “I am beyond forgiveness.”
And suddenly we begin writing conclusions that God never told us to write.
But we must also understand the difference between a biblical observation and a divine guarantee.
Sheshan's story does not promise that every earthly disappointment will be reversed.
Some faithful believers never receive the healing, marriage, children, financial relief, or reconciliation they long for in this life.
The Bible does not hide that reality.
Hebrews 11 describes people who experienced extraordinary deliverance and others who suffered terribly while remaining faithful.
God's faithfulness is not measured only by whether our circumstances improve.
His greatest promise to those who belong to Christ is not a trouble-free earthly life.
It is Himself.
His grace.
His presence.
His forgiveness.
His eternal kingdom.
And a resurrection hope that suffering and death cannot finally destroy.
That is why this obscure genealogy becomes even more meaningful when we place it within the larger story of Scripture.
Because 1 Chronicles begins by tracing generations, families, and tribes.
It reminds Israel of its history and identity.
And within the broader biblical story, the tribe of Judah carries special significance.
Genesis 49:10 associates Judah with royal authority.
Second Samuel 7 records God's covenant promise concerning David's royal house.
And the New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as the promised descendant of David, the Lion of the tribe of Judah.
Revelation 5:5 calls Him:
“The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David.”
But here is an essential distinction.
The particular line of Sheshan, Jarha, and Attai is not identified in Scripture as the direct ancestral line of Jesus Christ.
We must not claim that Jarha was an ancestor of Jesus when the biblical genealogies do not establish that.
The wonder is not that we can force every name into the Messiah's direct family tree.
The wonder is that the biblical record preserves a complicated and unexpectedly diverse human family history within the tribe from which the Messiah would come.
And the greater story of redemption reveals a Savior whose mercy is not restricted to one social class or one ethnic group.
The Gospel does not teach that everybody is automatically saved because of their ancestry.
It teaches that salvation is found in Jesus Christ.
Through His death and resurrection.
By grace.
Through faith.
And that is where the story becomes personal.
Because there is a deeper kind of exclusion than being overlooked by society.
There is the separation from God caused by sin.
You can have the right family name and still need forgiveness.
You can possess wealth and still be spiritually lost.
You can be respected in church and still hide a heart that has grown cold toward Christ.
You can know every worship song and still be resisting the Lord who calls you to repentance.
You can quote Scripture publicly while privately living in ways that contradict it.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing about spiritual pride is that it can make us believe we belong near God because we are better than somebody else.
But the Gospel destroys that illusion.
Romans 3:23 says:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” — ESV
All.
The powerful.
The poor.
The religious.
The rebellious.
The respected.
The rejected.
The person who appears to have everything together.
And the person who can barely get through the night.
We do not come to God boasting about our position.
We come acknowledging our need for mercy.
And then we discover something far greater than the continuation of an earthly family line.
We discover the possibility of reconciliation with God Himself.
Listen to the words of the apostle Paul in Ephesians 2:12–13.
He reminds Gentile believers that they had once been separated from Christ, strangers to the covenants of promise, and without God in the world.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turning points in the New Testament.
“But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.” — Ephesians 2:13, ESV
But now.
Two words that carry the weight of redemption.
You were far off.
But now.
You were without hope.
But now.
You were alienated.
But now.
Not because you purchased your way into God's favor.
Not because you earned a place through perfect behavior.
Not because you belonged to the right earthly family.
But because of Jesus Christ.
Because of His blood.
Because of His cross.
Because the Son of God did what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And Paul goes on to say in Ephesians 2:19:
“So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God.” — ESV
Members of the household of God.
Let those words settle into your heart.
For everyone who has trusted Christ, the greatest belonging is not a place at an earthly table.
It is reconciliation with the Father through the Son.
And the Greek language makes Paul's emphasis especially vivid.
In Ephesians 2:19, the word οἰκεῖοι (oikeioi) refers to members of a household or family.
Paul is describing the new relationship believers have through Christ.
They are no longer spiritual outsiders.
They belong to God's household.
Not because the Gospel ignores sin.
But because Jesus dealt with sin at the cross.
Not because God lowered His holiness.
But because Christ bore the judgment sinners deserved and rose again victorious.
Not because grace makes repentance unnecessary.
But because saving grace brings us into a new life where repentance, faith, and obedience become the response of a transformed heart.
And perhaps this is where the story reaches the person who has been reading quietly, feeling something begin to break inside.
Because you know what it is to feel unworthy.
Not merely because other people judged you.
But because you know what you have done.
You remember the lies.
The secret messages.
The bitterness you kept feeding.
The addiction you promised to leave behind.
The person you wounded.
The marriage you neglected.
The faith you slowly abandoned.
The prayers you stopped praying because you felt like a hypocrite.
You know how to smile at church.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to post a Bible verse.
But sometimes, when the house becomes quiet and nobody is watching, you wonder whether God could still welcome someone who has failed Him so many times.
Hear the Gospel.
Jesus Christ did not die for people who had already made themselves righteous.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — ESV
While we were still sinners.
Not after we fixed everything.
Not after we erased our past.
Not after we became impressive enough to deserve divine attention.
Christ died for sinners.
And when He rose from the dead, He demonstrated that sin and death would not have the final victory over those who belong to Him.
That does not mean sin is harmless.
It means forgiveness is available.
It does not mean we should continue in rebellion.
It means we can turn from rebellion and come to Christ.
It does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It means guilt does not have to remain our eternal master.
First John 1:9 gives this assurance:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — ESV
There is no need to pretend before a God who already knows the truth.
No need to perform strength while your soul is exhausted.
No need to defend the sin that is destroying your peace.
You can confess it.
You can repent.
You can turn to Jesus.
You can ask Him for mercy.
And you can begin walking in the light.
Perhaps that is the most important difference between a sentimental message and the actual Gospel.
A sentimental message says, “You are perfect just the way you are.”
The Gospel says, “You are deeply loved by God, and you desperately need the Savior who can forgive and transform you.”
A sentimental message says, “Never change for anyone.”
Jesus says in Mark 1:15:
“Repent and believe in the gospel.” — ESV
A sentimental message says, “Your past does not matter.”
The Gospel says your sin matters so seriously that Christ went to the cross, and His grace is so powerful that your past does not have to define your future.
This is the difference between self-affirmation and salvation.
Between being emotionally inspired for a few minutes and being genuinely reconciled to God.
And that is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not merely a beautiful phrase.
Because the scandal of human sin is real.
The shame is real.
The consequences are real.
The wounds are real.
But the grace of Jesus Christ is also real.
And His grace is not an excuse to remain unchanged.
It is the mercy that forgives and the power that calls us into a new way of life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.” — ESV
Notice the condition.
If anyone is in Christ.
The promise is not that every person will automatically receive a new life merely by feeling encouraged.
The promise belongs to those who are united to Jesus Christ by faith.
And that new life begins to change how we treat people.
If Christ welcomed us by grace, how can we despise someone because of their background?
If we have been forgiven, how can we refuse to acknowledge our own need for repentance?
If the Lord has shown mercy to us, how can we build our identity around humiliating others?

If God has made us members of His household, how can we continue treating our brothers and sisters in Christ as though they are spiritually inferior because they are poor, foreign, struggling, or socially insignificant?
And if we truly believe that the Gospel is good news, why would we want to keep it to ourselves?
This is where I want to ask you something.
Not as someone trying to collect a reaction.
But as one human being speaking to another.
What is the sentence you have allowed to become the ending of your story?
“I failed.”
“My marriage broke.”
“My child walked away from God.”
“I wasted too many years.”
“I fell into the same sin again.”
“I have nothing left.”
“I am too old.”
“I am too damaged.”
“I am not enough.”
Maybe you have repeated that sentence so many times that it no longer sounds like an opinion.
It sounds like your identity.
But your circumstances are not your Savior.
Your shame is not your Lord.
And your failures do not possess the authority to overrule the promises of Jesus Christ.
I cannot promise you that every broken relationship will be restored.
I cannot promise that every financial hardship will disappear.
I cannot promise that the life you imagined will unfold exactly as you hoped.
But I can point you to the Savior who promised never to cast out the one who comes to Him.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.” — ESV
Whoever.
That is an invitation broad enough for the person who has never entered a church.
For the believer who has wandered.
For the parent carrying regret.
For the young person trapped in secret sin.
For the exhausted minister.
For the person who looks successful but feels empty.
For the one who thinks they have crossed too many lines to return.
Come to Christ.
Not to a religious performance.
Not to an image you must maintain.
Not to a promise that you will never struggle again.
Come to the crucified and risen Savior.
Confess your sin.
Trust His mercy.
Submit your life to Him.
And learn to follow Him, one obedient step at a time.
And if you have already come to Christ but feel weary, remember that spiritual growth is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like opening your Bible when you would rather scroll.
Sometimes it looks like apologizing first.
Sometimes it looks like refusing the temptation you once welcomed.
Sometimes it looks like telling a trusted Christian, “I need help.”
Sometimes it looks like getting out of bed and praying through tears.
Sometimes it looks like returning to worship after a season of distance.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving someone while still wisely maintaining necessary boundaries.
Sometimes it looks like admitting that you cannot heal yourself and need both prayer and practical support.
Faithfulness is not always loud.
And genuine discipleship is not measured by how impressive your testimony sounds.
It is seen in a life increasingly surrendered to Jesus.
Now return with me to the genealogy.
Sheshan had no sons.
Jarha was an Egyptian servant.
Sheshan's daughter married Jarha.
Attai was born.
And the names continued.
The Bible does not tell us how every member of that family felt.
It does not reveal whether the marriage was celebrated, controversial, difficult, or joyful.
It does not give us permission to turn their lives into a fictional romance.
But it does preserve the names.
And that preservation invites us to remember that God's Word often includes people whom a hurried reader would never notice.
Sometimes we are so desperate for spectacular miracles that we overlook the quiet testimony of a continuing generation.
Sometimes we are so impressed by kings and warriors that we forget the people whose lives were recorded in only a sentence.
And sometimes we are so focused on the great names of Scripture that we forget the greater God who stands behind the whole redemptive story.
Because Jarha is not the hero of the Bible.
Sheshan is not the hero.
Attai is not the hero.
Neither are you or I.
Jesus Christ is the center of the Gospel.
He is the promised King.
The sinless Savior.
The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
The risen Lord.
The only mediator between God and humanity.
And the One who will return in glory.
The story of Sheshan's family may remind us not to mistake an apparent dead end for the whole story.
But only the Gospel can assure us that those who trust Christ will never face eternal condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” — ESV
No condemnation.
Not because our sins were imaginary.
But because Jesus truly saves.
And if these words have reached a place in your heart that you have been afraid to expose, do not rush past that moment.
Talk to God.
Tell Him the truth.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him for mercy.
If you need to repent, stop defending what He is calling you to surrender.
If you need prayer, do not suffer in isolation.
Not because writing a comment saves you.
Not because a public declaration replaces repentance or personal faith.
But because sometimes admitting our need for Christ is the beginning of a conversation we have avoided for far too long.
If you have experienced God's mercy and want to encourage someone who thinks their life is beyond repair, share a brief testimony of what Christ has been teaching you.
Your story may remind another person to seek the Savior.
You may never know who reads it silently.
The friend who has stopped attending church.
The family member who feels ashamed.
The believer who is struggling with hidden sin.
The person who has never understood the Gospel.
The exhausted parent.
The lonely young adult.
The person who has been asking God whether there is still hope.
Only Jesus saves.
But Scripture shared faithfully can point people toward Him.

We want this community to be a place where biblical truth matters more than popularity, where grace is never separated from repentance, and where people are encouraged to know Jesus Christ rather than merely admire religious content.
The purpose is simple.
To help believers open their Bibles.
To encourage struggling Christians.
To equip families.
To deepen discipleship.
To offer resources that point people back to Jesus Christ.
Not out of guilt.
And certainly not because God sells His favor.
Salvation is a gift of grace, and it cannot be purchased.
But Scripture does encourage believers to support faithful Gospel work through voluntary, generous giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.” — ESV
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows how believers supported Paul's ministry through material gifts.
That is a biblical pattern worth honoring.
Some believers may prayerfully choose to make that contribution part of their planned Christian giving.
You glorify Him through faith in Christ, worship, obedience, love, generosity, and a life surrendered to His will.
And for those who are willing and able, supporting faithful Christian teaching can be one meaningful expression of that devotion.
These items are not the reason to give.
They are simply a way of expressing appreciation to those who choose to stand alongside the ministry.
And if you are not in a position to contribute financially, please do not feel excluded.
You are still welcome here.
Read the Scriptures.
Use the free resources.
Pray for the ministry.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your place in the body of Christ.
It is to see people encounter the truth of Scripture, repent of sin, trust Jesus Christ, grow in holiness, and carry His Gospel into their homes and communities.
It will be whether we were faithful to the Lord Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that brings us back to the most unexpected lesson of this entire account.
Sheshan's name was preserved.
Jarha's name was preserved.
Attai's name was preserved.
Generation after generation followed.
But those names are not the final destination of the Bible's message.
They are part of a much larger Scripture that leads us to the God who creates, judges, redeems, and restores.
And the same Bible that records an Egyptian servant within a Judahite genealogy also announces a Savior who calls sinners from every nation to repent and believe.
So tonight, before you close this article, ask yourself one question.
Not “How can I make people admire my story?”
Not “How can I prove I am important?”
Not even “How can I guarantee that my life turns out the way I planned?”
Ask this instead.
“Lord Jesus, am I truly Yours?”
Because being remembered by history is not the same as being reconciled to God.
Having your name in a family genealogy is not the same as having eternal life in Christ.
And receiving human recognition is nothing compared with knowing the Savior.
If you have never trusted Him, come to Him today.
If you have wandered, repent and return.
If you are hiding, step into the light.
If you are weary, bring your burdens to Him.
And if you already belong to Christ, keep walking with Him even when the next chapter is not yet clear.
Sheshan had no sons.
Yet the genealogy continued.
Jarha was an Egyptian servant.
Yet his name was recorded.
And you may be looking at a chapter of your life that feels painfully unfinished.
But do not confuse an unfinished chapter with permission to abandon your faith.
You do not know every tomorrow.
You do not control every outcome.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But you can entrust yourself today to the crucified and risen Christ.
The One whose grace does not merely improve our reputation.
It reconciles us to God.
The One whose forgiveness does not merely cover public embarrassment.
It cleanses repentant sinners.
The One whose power does not merely give us a more inspiring story.
It raises the dead and promises eternal life to those who believe.
And long after the world forgets your achievements, your failures, your titles, and your disappointments, one truth will matter more than all of them.
The greatest miracle is not that your name becomes important to the world, but that through Jesus Christ, a sinner can be welcomed into the household of God.
